utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. May you please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Yes, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, my colleagues from the Prosecution, to all in the courtroom and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, with Nicholas Robson, representing General Rasim Delic, with our assistant, Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Good afternoon to you. Mr. Mundis. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon everybody in and around the courtroom. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: My name is Nermin Pesto.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pesto, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of March, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would lead the witness through his military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In 1980 and 1981, you performed the regular military service in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in September 1991, you left the JNA, having assumed the position of captain of the reserve?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Until May 1992, you worked in an organisation in Rogatica. Later on, you found out that it was the Patriotic League for which you were working?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in May 1992, you entered the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And after having held positions in the 1st Rogatica Brigade and the TO Kakanj, you became, in June 1993, an operations officer in OG Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in November 1993, you transferred to the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: From late 1993 until early -- until September 1997, you were chief of the Operations Centre of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I was the chief until 1997. You said "1994".

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I apologise. You were, from late 1993 until September 1997, in that position?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Having held several positions afterwards, you retired in 2004 from the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, holding the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to take you to your time when you arrived in the 3rd Corps in November 1993. Could you tell us, at that point in time, who was the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: General Enver Hadzihasanovic was in command at the time, and then in three or four days the commander was the late General Mehmed Alagic. Is there something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Alagic perform the function of 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: General Alagic was the corps commander from the beginning, from November 1993, until the 27th of March or the 6th of April, 1994, when Mr. Mahmuljin took over the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And at the end of the war, who was commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You confirmed that you had been head of the 3rd Corps Operations Centre. Who was your superior in mid-1995?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: My superior officer was Colonel Haso Ribo, G3 of the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To whom did Mr. Ribo report to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: To the chief of Staff, Colonel -- or -- yes, he was a colonel at the time, Kadir Juso [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last name of the gentleman you just mentioned, for the record?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Kadir Jusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many subordinates did you have as chief of the Operations Centre in mid-1995?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I had two officers at the time, and I had one operator. The operator would change, but what is important was that there were two officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you state the name of your two officers, your two subordinates?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Captain Safet Sivro and Captain Mirsad Caluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you very briefly describe the tasks of your 3rd Corps Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Operations Centre had as its main function the organisation and the control of the functioning of the internal and the guard service in the corps and in all the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Apart from the internal and guard service, were there any other functions performed by your Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The Operations Centre's more important function was to take part in the formation of forward command posts. We would draft the plans and prepare the documentation that would be then maintained at the corps' forward command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And with regard to the -- you stated the internal service -- or you were providing internal services, you said. What internal services were you providing, as the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: A small digression. You're talking about internal guard service. No, it's the internal or the interior service, implying the shift duties. The guard duty was something separate. That was doing the guard activities. If you're asking me about the interior service, it was the duty shift service. We had a management team on duty. This was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what would this internal duty shift service provide for services? What type of services would they provide?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The duty service would receive information, process information, and pass on information. When I say "information," I'm thinking of reports, regular, interim reports, telephone reports, and contacts of the duty officer who would be in the duty officer's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, in mid-July 1995, where were you stationed or where were you working at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Upon return from the operation to deblock Sarajevo, I was in Zenica. I was in Zenica thus at the beginning of July and then throughout the whole period until the end of the war I was at Zenica, at the main command post in the building of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you a document. Exhibit 494 will appear on your screen shortly. Having just established that you had been at the 3rd Corps headquarter in Zenica in mid-July 1995, I'm interested, when the document appears, whether you have ever seen that document. Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I saw it when I was preparing to testify with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: During preparation for my testimony, you showed me this document from the General Staff, and I confirmed that on the basis of that, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please turn off his microphone. We have problems hearing correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your last answer, please?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I saw this document during proofing with you a month ago in Sarajevo, when I was giving my statement. I cannot recall -- I told you at the time that I could not recall if I saw this document in 1997. But later, while working with you, I saw that I was drafting my own orders, the orders of the 3rd Corps Command to the subordinate units, on the basis of this order, meaning that I must have then seen this order at the time. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, you were. Could you just explain what own orders you then drafted, based on that document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: We made operational orders on the basis of this order, the order according to which the subordinate units would implement what the General Staff was requesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if we look at paragraph 1 of this document, it deals with the situation in Zepa; right? And paragraph 2 states that the front in Zepa should be relieved. And picking up on your own words, you said that you drafted an order to subordinate units. Could you explain, looking at number 1, what did this order you drafted to subordinate units entail?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Probably the same as this item or paragraph, or very similar. I cannot remember now what I wrote, but I probably wrote also that it was essential to immediately undertake combat throughout the front in the area of units of the 3rd Corps on the selected objects and axes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you. Only one microphone is needed, either the lapel microphone or the other microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we're having some microphone problems. It's not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So do you remember to which units you sent your orders?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: To all the units that were connected with us at the time. I really cannot remember now, but yesterday, during proofing, I saw that there were two operations groups, the 35th and 37th Divisions, and there were three independent brigades, the 303rd, 319th, and 330th Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you believe you had sent orders to them, implementing the order which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have document PT2260 shown to the witness. Are there some problems getting the document? PT -- or P02260, yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here it's a document from the 18th of July, 1995, at 2000 hours. If we could please go to the last page in the B/C/S just to look at the initials, because I'm interested in who drafted this document. Yes. We see here the initials "NP." Could you explain, what do the initials "NP" stand for?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Those are my initials, "NP," and this "/HD," it's the typist, Dervisa Heric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So am I right in assuming that at this point in time, you, as head of the Operations Centre, have drafted this document in performing your ordinary duties?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could look for a second at numbers 3 and 4 of the document. In B/C/S, it's the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here, first of all, in the upper right-hand corner, it's addressed to the General Staff in Kakanj. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you look at number 3 and 4, just an abstract, can you explain what you're reporting about here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It's a regular combat report, reporting to the superior command that the planned attack was realised in the area of responsibility of the 319th and the 330th Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And moving to number 1 and 2 of your report now, you're reporting here about the 35th Division; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain what you're reporting to the General Staff Kakanj here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Based on the report from the 35th Division, I made this report, and it states that forces of the 35th Division, in coordination with the El Mujahedin Detachment, carried out the necessary preparations and were expecting combat to begin. Should I read everything or can I just explain in brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you, Mr. Neuner, do you need both microphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't know how to switch one off. That's my problem. I can either unplug the one -- technically, I have a problem. I don't know how to switch one of the two off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This came from the audio-visual booth two days ago. They suggested this plan. And once you plug in the microphone, the lapel microphone, they inform me the standard microphone doesn't work, although the red light is on, but I had my doubts about whether this would be an effective way to proceed, but the AV booth is the one who came in and suggested this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem I have is that when you have both of them, I have an echo that I hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm fine to switch this one off, but I understood the suggestion from the AV booth was to especially wear this one. I'll switch it off then, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do that which will be most efficient for your purposes. We'll just have to bear the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I hope this works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hope so. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain why you're reporting to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: All reports did go to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Why did you not report to Sarajevo General Staff?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: That was the procedure. The General Staff was in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I tender this document, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 525.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to the next document. It's P02279.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have just informed us that you have reported that combat in the 35th Division should go on, and looking at this document now, I want to follow up on this very point. If we can scroll on the B/C/S a little bit down, please. Could you first of all tell me who drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: These are my initials. I probably wrote that order, because at the time I was the only operative in the Corps Command, in the G3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see, if we scroll up on the B/C/S a little bit, that it is from the 21st of July, so three days after the report we just discussed. If you look at number 2, the first sentence, please, you're reporting here: "The forces of the 35th Division started the attack combat operations according to the Proljece plan ..." Could you explain what the Proljece plan is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Each planned attack has its code, its secret name, its name. In this case, it was"Plan Proljece, spring," like the Operation T, Operation Farz, Operation Proljece. Actually, Proljece was not an operation, because it was done by the 35th Division, so it was not at an operation level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I have this document tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At what level was it, this one, now that it was not at the level of operations, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the level of a fight or combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We have seen the order of the General Staff. We have heard that you issued orders to subordinate units. We have seen now you have just reported on the 21st of July that the combat has started. Could you explain to the Chamber, once a combat has started, what role has the Operations Centre in the 3rd Corps while the combat is ongoing?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The Operations Centre received reports from subordinate units and had to inform the superior command about it. We would receive the information, process it, and then pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. So I want to deal with this exact point now by showing you a couple of documents relating to this combat going on in the 35th Division, documents which relate to the evolution of combat and how you report to your superior command, as you just stated. The first document is P02298. We see here it's a document from the 23rd of July, 1995. And if you look at the initials "BS," could you state who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It was probably the duty officer, the operations duty officer. There was a different one every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I didn't write this myself. I was probably off that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand, but who is the abbreviation "BS" standing for?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Sinad Biramovic. He was an operative who occasionally worked at G3, so these might as well be his initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if we look here at the first paragraph of that document, it talks about, inter alia, that the El Mujahedin unit routed the Vukovi Detachment. The El Mujahedin Detachment, together with the 1st Manoeuvre Battalion, the 7th Muslim -- 7th Brigade routed the Vukovi Detachment. Do you find this? It's in the first paragraph, starting with the first hyphen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. Just a second. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the witness could look at the document without the Prosecutor leading him to believe or say something that isn't in the actual document. It is being put to the witness that the El Mujahedin was together with these units, which does not faithfully reflect the substance of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It says here -- I agree now, I was misled myself. It says here: "The El Mujahedin Detachment ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Get the witness to read and let's get the evidence from the witness, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the first hyphen which mentions the El Mujahedin Detachment and the Vukovi Detachment, if you have a look at this, please. Could you explain, to which army did the Vukovi Detachment belong to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Probably the Serb forces, the Chetnik forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you look here at the place names, Cevaljusa, Nikolino Brdo, would you know where these places are located, in which AOR?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I have this document tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to the next document, P2316. I don't think that this is the document. 2316. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, looking at the initials, state first of all who has drafted it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: These are my initials, so I was probably the one who produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I want you to look at the second paragraph, starting with: "Snage Odrena." If you have a look briefly. It talks here again about Nikolino Brdo, Ravne and later Potsjelovo. Could you explain where was the combat which you were reporting about, in which zone's AOR, which unit's AOR?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the initials in the upper middle of the document, could you explain what these initials are meant?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I signed this document, personally, instead of the commander, Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic. This was done in the morning hours, and the reason was he was absent from the command post. The next morning, when he arrived at the Command, I showed him this document and he initialled it, because he had by now seen it. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I ask the document please be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to document P02342, the last report about combat activities I'm showing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here it's a document from the 29th of July, 1995, and we can see in the addressee list again, as in the previous documents, among others, Kakanj is the addressee. I'm interested in section 2 of the document, which is, I believe, on the second page of the B/C/S. There is a subheading "35th Division" there, and in English it is page 4. If you have a short look at this subject section, please. You were reporting here that El Mujahedin and the 328th Brigade move a forward defence line to two points, 702 and 552. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain, in whose units, AOR, this combat is taking place?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The 35th Division, within the 35th Division -- well, I'm not sure what the subdivision was in terms of areas of responsibility. You can probably find that in the documents of the 35th Division, in their plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We've seen now a couple of documents in which you report about ongoing combat activities. Could you explain, did you get any response from Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to another aspect of the combat occurring in the 35th Division AOR. Could you explain whether, during these combat activities, any prisoners of war had been taken, any materiel, or any documents have been seized?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't know. The documents that I looked at during my proofing contain references to those who were captured, but I didn't see any of those simply because I was in Zenica myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I didn't ask whether you have seen them but whether you know that prisoners had been taken or other items seized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I simply must object to this line of questioning and the general misdemeanor on the part of the OTP. Obviously, this is not the only witness. We've had this with several witnesses already. Witnesses say, "I never heard anything about POWs, I didn't know about those at the time," and then they say, "the Prosecutor showed me certain documents, this and that, and what we just heard as I was being proofed." I really don't get it. What is this supposed to mean? Does it mean that we, the actual parties, must confront witnesses with documents that they've never seen before, something they were entirely unaware of as all of this was happening, and then in chief the Prosecutor or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just make your objection and get to the point on the objection. What is your objection? You're objecting that this witness is being asked questions about things he knows nothing about? Make the point. It doesn't help to give a long lecture. You've got to give the basis of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, it is not my intention to lecture anyone. I am trying to point out that there is a very serious form of behaviour at work here that is unseemly for an international court of law like this. I wish to get my objection on the record in its entirety. I object to -- I object to such questions being asked of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which questions, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- given the fact that -- the last question about information concerning POWs. It is clear that the witness is expected to answer based on documents that he was shown during his proofing. It is furthermore clear that the witness has already told us he knew nothing about these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The only thing I wish to state is that I have only selected documents which were drafted by this witness, and in these documents there are certain features, including POWs, items seized, and documents mentioned, so I'm not basically asking him to talk about something he does not know about. I'm asking him to comment upon his own documents. I cannot exclude the fact that he has forgotten, in the meantime, about it, but I'm only showing him his own documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I find very surprising, Mr. Neuner, from your point of view. I've seen at least two documents that are drafted -- were drafted by this witness in which POWs are mentioned. You didn't ask him -- you did not draw his attention to those paragraphs. Now, when the documents are gone, you're asking him, and he gets the answer -- he gives you the answer that he gives you, you get an objection, because he now says he knows nothing, and yet his own reports talk about those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. I have the documents listed here, ready to go, and I thought I established, before I showed him individual documents, his general knowledge about these issues without leading him. This was actually my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but if you refer a witness to a document that he drafted and you ask him about the contents of that document, are you leading him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm not leading him. Just before doing this, I wanted to establish his general knowledge about POWs taken, MTS taken, and other issues, so this is, I think, in all fairness to the witness, giving him a chance to say something without showing him his own documents. I'm prepared to show him his own documents in any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But in these documents, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not -- well, I saw statements to the effect that Chetniks have been picked up. There was one that talked about 20, at least, that I saw, and you didn't refer this witness to the contents of the document, you just got him to look at the initials, who signed it, whose initials they are. You tendered it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will be prepared to follow Your Honour's advice for the following documents and see whether I get further objections or hopefully that I succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do. For the time being, this objection is upheld. Just do the things correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could PT or P02289 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So we see here this 2289 -- I believe it is a different document, to be honest. We had this document a moment ago. I'm sorry. This is the wrong document. I need 2289. Thank you. Yes. So we see here it's from the 22nd of July, 1995. It's in addition to the regular combat report. Could you, first of all, explain who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: My initials. Could you please bring the document up a little? I signed it. I was the officer in charge on that particularly -- on that particular operations duty team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I want you to look at the third-last paragraph from the bottom, or in the English it's the very last paragraph of the first page. Could you explain the entry you are making here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Based on a report by the 35th Division, and I had processed that report and adjusted it for the purposes of informing General Staff, the 35th Division informed us that they had processed documents captured from the 1st Prnjavor Brigade, their intelligence organ. They had questioned prisoners and realised that their forces had been decimated. Eventually, it reads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please be asked to read more slowly when quoting from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you quote again, and slower?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It reads that after processing the seized documents of the intelligence body of the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade and interviewing those captured, we learned that the forces of the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade had been decimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just stop you here, it talks about interviewing of captives. Do you know who interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fate of the persons who were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Well, much less even. I was up in Zenica. I didn't hear anything about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you get, from the General Staff in Kakanj, any response relating to what you reported about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't remember. It has been a very long time. I don't know if anything happened about this. If so, it was probably down the security line or through the intelligence organs. However, it was the established practice, following a report that was submitted, to review anything. In particular, sometimes there would be orders about something that had gone awry. As for this, in particular, I don't think so. I can't say either way, whether anything happened or, in fact, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wish to tender the document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a bit, Mr. Neuner, because the Presiding Judge just invited you to be a little more careful in discussing the issues with the witness, and the last sentence of the part that he read out seems to suggest that there has been some sort of a disagreement with the El Mujahid Detachment, who apparently burned some of the papers. So the issue that raises out of this is, of course, whether anyone from the El Mujahid Detachment was involved in the questioning of prisoners of war and whether they were involved in the seizure and destruction of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe I have tried to clarify who was interviewing and didn't get an answer for which unit did it, but I want to ask the second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have heard Your Honour Judge Harhoff. He was interested in who was involved in the seizure and destruction of the documents. It says "burning" here.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The report by the 35th Division says that this was done by fighters from the El Mujahedin Detachment. Whether they were there or not, I don't know, I can't comment, because I wasn't actually over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I ask that the document please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi wanted to ask something. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: 22nd of July. I want to move on to document 2319 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see it's a document from three days later, 25th of July, also sent to Kakanj, and I'm interested in the last page, namely, the question who drafted the document, or the second-last page, please. Could we go to the second-last page in B/C/S, please. Scroll down a little bit, please. Thank you. Who has drafted it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I am the final author. When I say "the final author," by this time we had started making reports in each of the departments, G3, the corps department. Item number 6, for example, it was the security department that drafted that. They provided him with that particular portion, and the document was signed by Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the number section, information provided by the security department, it talks here about processing of captured members. Could you explain what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the English a little bit enlarged, please? We can't see what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Previous page actually. In English, it should be page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, take us to the relevant page, so that when you read, we can read with you, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It's page 7 right now. We need to go to page 6, yeah, and below, the section "Security." Thank you. And we see the first paragraph here mentioning processing of captured members. In the second line, Your Honour, under number 6, it talks about processing of captured members of the platoon of Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain what is meant here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The reference here is probably to statements being taken from the Muslims who, as the document shows, were from Prnjavor. Processing means the taking of statements in order to obtain maximum intelligence and security information on the enemy. That's what processing means, but this is in error. They were not captured. They were, in fact, set free, because they had been used by the aggressor to perform labour. This was written by a fellow officer of mine from the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you know his name?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I can't remember his name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, based on this explanation, I would seek to tender the document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have one last document relating to POWs and Bosniaks, P02324. The document we just saw was from the 25th of July, and this document, if we can maybe in the B/C/S go to the second page just for a second, we see here it is dated a day later, the 26th of July. And to help you familiarise yourself with the document, if we could go in B/C/S to the last page for a second to check for the initials of the drafter. Could we scroll down, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You see here the initials are "NP." Who has drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. So I want to take you in that document, in B/C/S, to page 5, namely, its first paragraph. And in English, corresponding to that, is page 9, the second paragraph. We see here, in the second sentence, "a total of 11 surviving members of work platoons of Muslim ethnicity were captured together with 12 Chetniks, as well as one T-55 tank." Could you explain where, in whose AOR, these people have been captured?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 2, and then I can see page 4, but that's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I said page 5 of the --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Perhaps what I need to look at is page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it page 3 in the B/C/S? On page 5, actually, it says "Page 5." Yes. I think it's the first paragraph here.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. We see here the 12 Chetniks and the 11 persons of Muslim or Bosniak ethnicity. Could you explain where -- in whose AOR were these people captured?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: This paragraph refers to the 35th Division, and then after that you have the area of responsibility of the 37th Division. So this must have been in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you see here for the first time numbers mentioned.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Twelve Chetniks and 11 surviving members. Could you explain -- we talked before about Muslims from work platoons. Are we talking about one and the same group or are we talking about different groups here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Probably the same or it's a coincidence that there were 11 on the other side, but it was in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. I don't know if those 11 that we mentioned earlier -- or perhaps this was in some other place. I don't know. It's not possible to conclude if the 11 mentioned previously are the same as these 11 now. We don't have any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Nevertheless, I wish to tender the document, based on the explanations given, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, what role did the Operations Centre play when high guests or distinguished guests were visiting the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The Operations Centre was in charge of preparing the operations room or the briefing room, meaning that you would draw the name tags, indicate where people would be sitting. If the commanders were at the -- if the meetings were at the commander's office, then we were not there; only if the meetings were held in the operations room, then we would be doing these preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who was superior to Mr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The commander of the army, General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Rasim Delic visited the 3rd Corps in 1995 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With whom would Mr. Delic meet if he would come to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: With the commander, and if the commander was not there, the chief of Staff. If both of them were absent, then with the deputy commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When, if at all, did you see Mr. Delic visiting?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I saw him several times over the period of those three years, 1993, 1994, 1995. When I say "several times," I mean three or four times a year; not frequently, but he would come to the Corps Command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We saw that in your documents, a couple of times El Mujahedin units -- the El Mujahedin Detachment was mentioned. Did you ever meet a member of that detachment during the war?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Like I said to you yesterday during the proofing, the first time I saw two or three members of the Mujahedin movement, I was with General Nehru Ganic, and we received those three in the duty operations room, those three Mujahid members. And I think we discussed then the transfer of the Mujahid movement from the -- detachment from the Bosnia Operations Group to the 3rd Corps. I think that was the one time that I saw those three Mujahedin come. We didn't really have any access later. As I said, the El Mujahedin Detachment, we did send orders to them, but none of us ever went there to check what the situation was there in the field; are they organised, do they have documents. They never reported to us. They never sent reports about anything that they requested. They were their own, as we would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So apart from that visit of the three gentlemen, did you at any point in time again encounter a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get some clarification here, what is the Bosnia Operations Group from which the El Mujahedin Detachment was transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't say "Operations Group Bosna." The Operations Group Bosna was a forerunner of the 35th Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "Bosanska Krajina, I didn't say "Operative Group Bosnia." These are two operations groups. Operations Group Bosnia -- Bosna is in Zavidovici, and that is where the 35th Division was formed from. Where the Mujahedin were before they came to the 3rd Corps, they were in the Operations Group or the operations group zone of the Bosanska Krajina group in Travnik, I think they were in some village near Travnik, I believe. I don't know how many of them there were. I also don't know the exact date when they came to us. Are you satisfied with the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not quite. Maybe it was a question of translation, because what was written -- what's written here was what you said, they had been transferred from the Bosna Operations Group, but you've explained what the difference is. My question to you now is: Of what army, if at all, was the Bosanska Krajina Group near Travnik a unit of, if it was indeed a unit of an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Operations Group Zapad and Bosanska Krajina were units of the 3rd Corps. By forming the 7th Corps, they then were transferred to the 7th Corps, on the 4th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you. Are you then saying that the El Mujahedin Detachment was being transferred from the Bosanska Krajina Group to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it has been transferred from a unit of the 3rd Corps to be subordinated directly to the 3rd Corps without coming underneath a unit within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you state who was the 7th Corps commander in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The late General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you have mentioned OG Bosna also in your response. To whom was OG Bosna subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: To the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to come to my last topic relating to September 1995. Where were you, in the first half of this month, employed?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the first half of September 1995, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: At the Corps Command in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your subordinate Safet Sivro, where did he work the first half of September 1995?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: After returning from the Forward Command Post Orahovo near Sarajevo, he went to the corps' forward command post in Zavidovici right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To do what?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: An operative officer, operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Working in the IKM of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Where was Haso Ribo working in this time period, your superior?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: At the IKM also in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe it is time for the break. I'm two to three minutes from being done, maybe five, so I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have used one hour 15 minutes of your one hour. You realise that. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to take you directly to PT2 -- please?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may provide a clarification. Earlier, when we were talking about the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina, I have no information. I don't know that they were part of the Mujahedin, that they were part of the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group. I don't know if they were their members. I'm afraid that from my statement earlier, you could interpret that they were in the establishment formation of the 7th Corps or the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina, but this is something that I don't know. All I know is that they were from the environs of Travnik and then that they came to the village of Sarici, I think, near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pesto, I am not sure I understood exactly. When did you see these three members of the El Mujahid Detachment and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, then they were talking about whether it was the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group, so it was in the summer, or at the end of the winter, or in the spring of 1994. I'm not sure whether they were from the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina, that zone, or whether that was already the 7th Corps, when they came to the village of Sarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that is where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. No, I didn't. I saw those three who came to the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who did they come to talk to at the Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were received by the chief of Staff, Nehru Ganic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was it him only they spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the duty officer's room, there was only myself and Mr. Ganic. As for what we talked about, please believe me when I say that I don't know now, and I don't have that in my notes. I don't have any information in my notes, what we talked about. That's why I couldn't find the exact date when we spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But they only spoke to you and Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Mr. Ganic. I was just present as the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to talk about September 1995, but since you just referred back to 1994 and the El Mujahedin Detachment, I want to show you a document, PT1740. Maybe this helps you recalling certain events. Actually, the date is not exactly visible. It says here in the English translation "3rd of May, 1994", and if we scroll down to see who drafted the document, could you tell us whether you recognise the document and who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: They're my initials, so it was probably me, I drafted it, because my handwriting is in the paragraph marked "1." I wrote something in additionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At 2(b), it mentions here -- this is, I think, from May 1994, the document. It mentions here also the El Mujahid Detachment. Do you recall the incident or why you drafted this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: What, the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I mean, why you drafted this. It refers here to several units, Ogiceva, 330 Light Brigade, 319th Mountain Brigade, El Mujahid Detachment and so on. Do you recall why you drafted this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Not specifically, no, but I can comment on this, that the El Mujahid Detachment is in OG3 North, is part of it, because it's in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain where the headquarter of OG3 North is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: At the 3rd Corps IKM at Postojna. This is a settlement before Topcic Polje near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask that the document please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to go back to September 1995 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You explained to us where Mr. Sivro was before the break, and if you look at PT2566 for a moment -- excuse me, 2561. Exhibit 394, I'm told. Yes. And I'm interested in entry number 1, which is, I believe, on the second -- the third page in the B/C/S, as well as on the third page in the English. Entry number 9 in English. In English, we see entry number 1 here. We need the next page, I believe. Could we in English go to the next page, please. Yes, it can stay like this. It is an entry we see from the 10th of September, 1995, at 0030 in the morning, and could you first of all look at the signature on the right-hand side. Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Of my operative, Safet Sivro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain what the entry relates to? Could you explain what is happening here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Captain Safet Sivro here from the Forward Command Post, called me. I was the duty operations officer at the 3rd Corps Command, so by chance my name happens to be there because I was on duty over there. And he asked that the intelligence unit implements the order from the General Staff that arrived at the IKM, and not because it came as a preparatory order. As far as I know, the order always went via Zenica. Here, it was probably a routine assignment, because every other day we would provide important aggressor targets because the NATO bombing was underway. So it could not be something that could be linked to the operation that was going to ensue, this particular information, and it was forwarded on from Zenica because Ekrem Alihodzic, who was looking at the mail, knew that in the intelligence sector there were only one or two officers who could not resolve that, so he sent that to the chief of the intelligence section at the IKM. And then, in turn, he ordered the -- actually, the corps commander ordered Safet Sivro to call the duty operations officer to finish this assignment in Zenica. These were probably just routine tasks that were not related to the operation. This is my conclusion about why he had called me, but I cannot remember the particulars about when he called me and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No problem. Did you follow up and contact the intelligence officer, because that's what Mr. Sivro appears to have in mind?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to show you the last document. It's PT2566. This entry was from the 10th of September. The document is from a day later, you will see. First of all, whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we look in the English, we see it says: "Assistant Commanders Briefing." Could you explain what an assistant commanders briefing is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: These are regular briefings of the assistant commander, reporting to the commander or the acting commander about the activities in the sections, the intelligence, operations, morale, personnel, security, finance, legal affairs and logistics, all those sectors, and at the end would be the garrison affairs. The briefings were on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and these were regular briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And where were these briefings held?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: At the commander's office at the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. So you're reporting here the situation of your own forces. Could you explain what you're doing here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: After the intelligence officer informs about the enemy activities over the past two days, then I report and inform the deputy commanders about our forces and of the tasks of the G3 sector that are connected to other departments or sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to turn to the first remark made by Nermin Prijic. Could you first of all explain who is Nermin Prijic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Prijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who is -- in which field of work was Mr. Nermin Prijic working?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: He was the desk officer for intelligence, in the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: He is reporting here, in the first line, that about 100 Chetniks remain encircled in Pejanovici sector. Could you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Based on his information and information that came through the intelligence organ's information channel and the operations channel, meaning the regular and interim reports received by the officer, he received information that 100 Chetniks were encircled in the Pejanovici area. "Encircled" means that they were surrounded or encircled. I don't know whether the number of 100 is the correct number or whether the sector is correct or not. I can't know that. But, anyway, that is the information that he presented at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: About which AOR -- about which unit's AOR is Mr. Prijic reporting?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: About the operation that was afoot in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I show you a map of the wider area, would you be in a position to find Pejanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If please the map from Court binder number 12 could be shown. The ERN is 0618-6712.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While this is being -- before this is being shown on the screen, could you tell us when these briefings would take place, at what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: In the morning, 8.00, half past 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Prijic is reporting this, then, at about 8.00, half past 8.00 in the morning; yeah?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look on this map, would you find Pejanovici sector?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The map's unclear. Can we zoom in, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Actually, if we could --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: To the right -- I think this is the wrong map. We need the map with Pozovici, which is northeast of Vozuce -- northeast of Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We could also -- okay. As it is -- I just see here the location is not shown. If we scroll down a little bit in the map, if you have a second look at it now, please.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, Pejanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If he could please get a Stelo so he could encircled it.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I see you have marked the location of Pejanovici. Could you mark a "1" next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask the map please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Before I ask that the document be tendered:

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain the significance -- or how was the reaction in the room when it was announced that 100 Chetniks would be encircled in this sector of Pejanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: This was very good news for our morale, very, very good news for our forces. It means that we inflicted a military defeat on the enemy and that we were about to liberate a part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain which forces managed to encircled the Chetniks? Which army managed to encircle?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't know. Our forces that were involved in the operation, the forces of the 3rd Corps. I do know that, but specifically as to the exact unit that was there, I don't know. I wasn't there, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But units of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I ask that the document please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. I'll be asking you questions on behalf of the Rasim Delic Defence team. Could you please speak as slowly as possible so that everything gets recorded. It is in the nature of cross-examination, as such, that you will be able to answer a great deal of my questions with a simple "yes" or "no." Should you require any further explanations, please say so.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have that much time, I will ask you directly about issues related to the role and functioning of the Operations Centre of which you were head; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you had very few people working for you there, as you said; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had two administrators or desk officers and several people who occasionally helped out with that; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, two administrators, desk officers, and a stenographer, as well as an operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that as head of the Operations Centre, or at least that was my understanding of what you had said, you had the responsibility of organising the work of the Operations Centre at the command post and many of the forward command posts and observation posts of the commander throughout 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that to cover a number of forward command posts, and I am putting to you which ones specifically, during the Farz operation, Klek, Luca, Kumanista, Stavci, Natron and Postojna, I think that post was mentioned, too, right, and then another two, commanders' observation posts, plus the principal command post, the main command post in Zenica, would I be right that given the shortage of manpower, it was very difficult to effectively cover all of your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just so that everybody understands, I think it is necessary for you to explain to us a number of issues that have to do with the functioning of the centre. This is for our benefit, so that we may understand what sort of documents were being produced there and what it was, generally speaking. Let me ask you this first: It's true, isn't it, that you were in charge of keeping planning documents primarily; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Work plans, a log of daily orders, and a duty roster; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you kept records, operations log, war log, minutes from briefings such as the ones we looked at earlier today; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This also included reports or information documents; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regular and interim reports; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Analysis of the implementation of monthly plans?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And analysis of combat readiness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Analysis of combat readiness, that is something we did, because I was the only one there at the time, at the Corps Command. I mean, normally this sort of document would be produced by the Department for Planning and Monitoring Combat Operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this additional elucidation. Let me ask you this now: The planning documents thus you mentioned and that you enumerated, those were prepared and produced, but in practical terms, amid all the fighting and combat, one often had to give them up in some ways, right, or there were aberrations from these reports?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The situation in this part of Bosnia, the Ozren and Vozuca area, for example, during the Farz operation, was such that the planning documents could simply not be kept on a regular basis; is that right? Things happened ...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: For the most part, we tried to go on producing these documents. I don't know about regularity, though. It's difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the gist of my question. Amid much fighting and combat, it was impossible to keep neat and regular documents, in terms of planning documents; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: That's right, it is just as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you something about these records, such as, for example, operations logs, war logs. We had been looking at a number of those during this trial. You were head of the Operations Centre. Do you agree with me that the operations logs, for example, or war logs were not priority documents, were not a priority for the Operations Centre; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The operations log was, to some extent. As for the war log, it was something that one of my clerks did, but this would normally get done two or three months post facto. Sometimes a day or two would be skipped in the war log when the desk officer was away. Those days would simply not get recorded at all. The war log that we kept was not kept on a daily basis, because people were busy elsewhere and there was nobody around to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please elaborate on this? My understanding was this: Daily entries were made into the war log, whatever was happening at the time, but that is in fact not true at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So sometimes several days went by before someone eventually sat down to it and recorded something based on their memory; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Not then, not necessarily based on their memory. They would get old reports and they would extract the meaning from them. This would normally include a brief description of the situation on a particular day. This might be recorded two or three months later. I realised at one point, for example, that it wasn't being kept, I would tell my desk officer to go back to it and get the job done, then he would update the whole thing. And then I would forget about it for a while again and he would keep on doing the same thing, but the document was not being regularly updated at the 3rd Corps level.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I wish we had a copy of that document available now so we could check closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: As you were being proofed for your testimony, was such a document ever shown to you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Not document. It's actually a book, a 500-page book, and I wasn't shown that, the war log.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you were being proofed, were you shown that or not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will now go back to my previous topic. Witness, please, it is true, or at least that's what I understand you to be saying, that certain persons were entering information into this war log, and it depended entirely on them, regardless of whether we are talking about the operations log or the war log, what sort of information would be recorded; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, you're entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This information being entered into the operations log or the war log was, in fact, entered by the operations duty officer, whoever happened to be there; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct, sir, these people were not actually physically present when all of this was happening; somebody was informing them about what was going on? I mean the operations logs and the war logs, not the regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The war log was something that was kept at the Corps Command, and the entries that were made were made in a chronological order reflecting developments across units, the Command and so on and so forth. It was often the case, however, that entries were made at a later stage additionally. As for the operations log, another document that was kept at the time, this was a compulsory document kept at forward command posts and back at the Command, and it is the duty operations officer who is in charge of this document, whoever happens to be on duty. They get information by telephone, and then this gets recorded. In 95 per cent of the cases, the officer gets information by telephone, and then this information gets recorded, without verifying whether information is, in fact, true or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The operations log, the war log, these two are official documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct, these actually had to be stamped, they had to be sealed at the end of each and every one of these documents there would be an official stamp, seal; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes. Once these eventually got filed, the documents were stamped or sealed. Every time you have a book that is kept, you need to somehow complete it, and this is normally done by putting a seal on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just tell me what this means, to complete a book or a document? You have the last entry for a particular day, for example, so this is then ratified. A line is drawn under it, marking the end of that log. There needs to be a stamp, and this needs signing by whoever confirms that this is the end of that particular document, and then there is a stamp. Is that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: That is the procedure, but I'm not sure we put the stamp there, not always at the end, but the general procedure is, indeed, what you suggest. A filing number is given, a date is given. The document is signed. And that's it. I'm not sure if you are referring specifically to a document that you have in mind, but you know that this was always the case, the procedure was always the same every time records were kept, especially in relation to forward command posts. A line is drawn under a document, the date is recorded, for example, the 18th of September, 1500 hours. You might get to read something like that. A line is drawn, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Trial Chamber how this is ratified, how this is confirmed? Where do we see that on a given document? Is it the same place where the line is drawn?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's where it's supposed to be. I'm not sure which specific document you have in mind, but someone signs it and then certifies this by putting a seal on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it's the person's signature that gets certified?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of whether we're talking about the operations log or the war log, about the register or whatever, we have a situation, for example, developments on a given day, a certain person hands over, another person takes over, comes on duty, and then there is a blank that runs into 20 or more pages with no entries, and then at the end we see: "Certified by," "This book contains 35 lists," and so on and so forth. Is something like that possible or did this have to be certified, the very end of all entries made to a particular book?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: When the book is opened, at the end it's written that the book has so many pages, and then it's certified either by the chief of Staff or the commander of the chief of the office. This is done at the end of each book that is opened. Even the work books that we used, the procedure is the same. Sometimes pages were skipped. I know in the war log or diary, pages were skipped. That's what we did in our books.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, just one moment. The number of pages is certified precisely so that somebody would not rip a page out, copy something or add something. Pages should not be ripped out from that book?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No, no. In no case, yes. This was not something that should have been allowed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if it said that a book had 95 pages, it had to have had 95 pages?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: In 1995 as well as now, today, it would still have to have the same number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, very well.
