So I am correct when I say that the last entry, at the end of the last entry, has to be something that bears a stamp and the signature of the person indicating that that was the end of the data entries, so that something else could not be added on subsequently?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should have been. I'm not sure if this was certified by a stamp, but I would always, for example, sign my own books at the end. I don't know if a stamp was used. I don't know if I had the right to use a stamp or not, but I used my own signature to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it had to have been entered that the book was completed and that the fact that it was completed was something that Nermin Pesto certified of?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask you something about information and the accuracy of information that was being entered into the war or the operations logs or diaries. Do you agree that the information and its accuracy directly depended on the way the person that was receiving the information -- or actually that was sending the information first about the event, and then the person that was receiving that information, understood that information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it also directly depended on the knowledge and the experience of that person?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, particularly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it depended on whether the person had military training, would they understand properly what they were supposed to write down?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you one of these logs or diaries. Can we please show the witness Exhibit 394. Your Honours, I expected, and I wrote that in the letter to my colleagues in the Prosecution, that they would need to bring the original of this logbook, but in any case perhaps Mr. Pesto can tell us, without looking at the original. Perhaps he can give us some explanations, in any case. Mr. Pesto, please, it seems here we don't have any -- if I can ask my colleague Mr. Mundis about the original that we had yesterday. That was this original of this document. Does the Prosecution still have this document with them here in the courtroom now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No. Those documents need to be returned to the evidence vault every evening. I wasn't aware that she'd -- that my learned colleague wanted the document again today. We can send an e-mail out and try to get it here. It will take some time to get it signed out of the evidence vault. But if she wants it, we can certainly attempt to have it. I'm sure we'll have it at the beginning after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. In connection with this document, I'm going to go back behind this document after the break, but still when we have this document on our screens, I would like the witness to look at a page of this document. This is page 3 of the Bosnian version, and it's the same page, actually, the same page 3 that the Prosecutor showed the witness earlier. Entry number 9. Yes, that was all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you gave us an explanation about this document. All I want you to know is what I'm going to be asking you about. It says an order arrived from the General Staff on furnishing information on important aggressor military targets, and you explained to us that this was something that was routine. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't, but I assume that this was a routine task.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you if you recall testifying to this effect earlier today in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Your Honours, if at this point in time the witness can look at document D503. Can we put this document away, please. I'm going to go back to it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We saw a little bit earlier, and that's why I showed you this document -- do you recall that this was a document before that you saw for the last time? This was an entry for the 10th of September, 1995. You saw this in this diary; isn't that correct? And now I would like you to look at this document and to read it to yourself. Do you agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam Vidovic. Is this document dated the 10th of September or is it the 9th of September? It looks like -- you're talking about an entry here, not the date. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to say this document is connected to that entry of the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that this is a document of the General Staff in Kakanj of the 9th of September, 1995, requesting the dispatch of information via an order of the Commands of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and the 7th Corps and these divisions? I would like you to look where it says: "For the purposes of completing and updating information on the aggressor forces, urgently submit the coordinates of the aggressor's important military targets in your area of responsibility, such as ..." and then they are enumerated. Your Honours, I would just like to scroll down the document so that you can follow. Do you agree that it says here that it was processed under KZ cryptographic protection on the 9th of September, 1995, at 2207 hours; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Corps Commands are giving a deadline here for the implementation of that particular task?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, it's correct, isn't it, that at that time -- Your Honours, at this point in time, because of the information that we are going to refer to, I would like to move into private session. I'm not sure that it would be wise to put questions like this in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at this entry for the 10th of September, 1995, which we looked at a little bit earlier. I think that that's page 3 of the Bosnian version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you again, just look at the date here. This entry bears the date the 10th of September, 1995, and do you agree that this was at 0030 hours, right after midnight?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and the task had to be implemented by 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. So that document that I showed you of the General Staff of Kakanj is directly connected with what is ordered to you in this entry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to tell us a little bit more about the reporting documents. This one can be put away, the document that is on the screen. We had the opportunity to see, and this is something that the Prosecutor showed you today, we saw regular and interim reports for which you've said were sent from the corps -- or actually they were sent from the corps to the superior command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, in order to understand -- in order for all of us in the courtroom to understand, because we lack military training and we did not work with the military, I would like to ask you to clarify the following: It's correct, isn't it, that you personally did not -- or any person in the Operations Centre did not -- the person drafting that report, it would be wrong to believe that that person is the author of that text; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the text that you draft as a combat report is actually something that you receive from the subordinate unit, and then you put it all together, several reports like that from different units, and then you compile one report on combat actions, which you then forward to the superior command; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So to simplify all of that, in your Operations Centre, the operations duty officer sits. Simply, he receives this report, and he does not check the information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He processes it -- go ahead. You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Especially if he sees something that something is not quite right or if he has doubts about the accuracy of the information, he would check whether it was correct or not by telephone. He has the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the large volume of work that they had, what do you think, did they check this information?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I believe that they did not. During proofing, I told the Prosecutor that unfortunately -- well, my commander is here and I can say that there were cases when reports that were sent to the superior command were even done by messengers. They would copy what happened the day before. I mean, things like that happened. There were different officers, trained and those who did not have any training. There were lazy and there were diligent officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I don't understand. What does the "doing by messengers" mean when you say, "My commander is here and I can say that there were cases when the reports that were sent to the superior command were even done by messengers"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that after 12 or 15 years my commander finds out only now that reports were sometimes produced by messengers, couriers in the units. The duty officer tasks a courier, a messenger, with doing this -- I'm not sure what to call them, a messenger, and they put it together, they put the gist there, and then the other guy tells him to type it up for him and off he goes. I tried to find a way around this by introducing the following procedure, and this received the support of the brigadier, the chief of Staff. Everyone in the department had to verify their own input, and that's when better quality reports, if I may put it that way, started being produced. I hope that I have now clarified sufficiently for your purposes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that point. When you say they copied what happened the day before, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, believe me, there were reports that I checked myself a day or two later, a Tuesday, for example, and then the report reads: "Given the fact that yesterday was a day of, the situation at the unit commands remained unchanged." And the previous day, for example, was a working Monday. I remember that. And I also remember the name of the officer who actually wrote this, but he asked me to please not mention his name here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will not force you to mention his name here. Okay. So, in other words, he just repeats what was reported the previous day; he's not reporting today's report? He copies what was recorded yesterday, a report which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- he already gave yesterday, he repeats it today. Okay, now I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you were physically present there, do you remember that -- do you agree that the 3rd Corps was facing problems with inaccurate reporting by subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Certain units inappropriately amplified their own success in terms of capturing POWs or MTS and such like; am I right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 303rd Brigade was actually dismissed or replaced because of untruthful reporting. I think it was sometime in 1994 or early 1995. Stojanovic was the name of the commander, I believe. He was reporting during the clashes with the HVO that they had shifted some lines, that they had taken a strategically-important hill or elevation, but they never specified. It was all just about him obtaining more ammunition. It was about him informing other people that he had carried out an attack, whereas in actual fact he hadn't, not at all. There was a lot of amplifying and exaggerating, various issues that were being reported, in order to improve combat morale but also because some people were simply not familiar with the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the commander of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Madam Vidovic, may I ask that you pause a little bit after the witness has answered, can you do the same, because the interpreters come after you and they finish some time after you, and if you now then carry on speaking, you overlap with him. The interpreter said he didn't hear the last part of your last answer. Can we finish that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke in the last part of your answer about how reports were amplified and exaggerated, various issues being blown out of proportion that were being reported on, and you said something else. Do you remember what?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I mentioned the Command of the 303rd, and there were other cases about that. This was about inaccurate or erroneous reporting, false reporting, if you like, under quotation marks, because we or the duty operations officer didn't know whether the information was in fact true or not, and there was a lot of exaggerating. As I was being proofed, I told the Prosecutor, when the intelligence officer said 100 Chetniks are surrounded, as soon as I heard of this, I told the Prosecutor that they should drop half of those, 100 divided by 2, in other words, because I simply wasn't certain that they were feeding me accurate information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then on what basis would you think, then, there were 50 and not hundred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm generalising. When I was receiving information on a daily basis and an intelligence officer, for example, would tell me there were 50 of them, we would divide it by 2. "Take some and leave some," that's what we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you, yourself, added to the confusion. You realise this? Maybe you should have divided by three, maybe by four. Maybe you should have multiplied by ten. Now, you're adding to the confusion by tampering with the data. You realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we didn't tamper with information. We just passed it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you reduce 100 to 50, if you say "divide it by two," you're tampering, aren't you? Or let me back off. You're saying -- in conversation, you say, "Okay, it cannot be 100, it should be 50," but in your reporting, you pass on the figure 100 that you received; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I'm sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, too. I think there's been a misunderstanding. As I was being proofed, I said that I wouldn't take anything that intelligence officers were saying at face value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we understand. You just didn't believe them, but you passed the information as it came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you refused to take this at face value simply because you had ascertained yourself that there had been various cases and issues that had been exaggerated in the past; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, probably, but it's difficult for me to say now because you've got me a little mixed up, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now: You remember the problem of false information or inaccurate reporting reaching such levels that the morale department had to hold a briefing about this that was attended by General Delic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: This main factor occurred several times. I'm not sure if Mr. Delic was there, but this subject was discussed several times and commanders were invited to go and see General Mahmuljin, to be subjected to criticism for doing that. They'd be out on their ear, that's what he was telling them, and they stopped doing that. I'm not sure if Delic was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In other words, General Mahmuljin would not just be making something like this up unless obviously there was a real problem like that in the 3rd Corps, an actual problem?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: He was 100 per cent right in being adamant about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll now move on to something else. You were shown today quite a number of documents about reports, the reports that we are now talking about, the reports that were being submitted to the Kakanj command post. You remember seeing that; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that this was how it worked: The reports, combat reports, were delivered to the Kakanj command post, and this was something that was envisaged in a specific order; right?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, at this point in time I would like the witness to look at a set of documents marked as D446. This contains a number of reports on combat operations. The OTP, in fact, confronted the witness with these documents today, but I do want the witness to look at a number of other documents, too, primarily page 1 of this set. I think this is the page, and if I could ask the witness to please just pay close to attention to the portion mentioned by the Prosecutor. You said that you wrote and dispatched this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just please look at the portion in reference to units of the 35th Division, and of course you see that the El Mujahedin unit is described here as being primarily in charge of the task at hand, and you also confirm for us that this document would eventually be sent to the General Staff, the command post of Kakanj. You see that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is about carrying out actually combat operations on the 18th of July; right? All right. Could the witness now please go to page 3 of this set. Page 3. Just a moment, please. All right. This is page 4. Could we please have page 3 of the B/C/S, or the previous page, if that's any easier. Right, thank you. Witness, do you agree that this is a document by the Army General Staff, Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The Administration for Operational Planning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th of July, 1995, and it's a report on the situation in the BH theatre of war on the 18th of July, 1995. Could you please now just look at the addressees? Do you not agree that it reads the president of the Presidency, the army commander and so on and so forth? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've seen this report. I'm not asking you about the way it was dispatched. I'll be asking you about the information that you looked at a while ago which had to do with the El Mujahedin Detachment. And one thing I would like to ask you: You agree that this information would normally be part of the report concerning the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you please locate that part, "Activities of the Aggressor," and then if we could go to the next page, please, if that can -- if the witness can be shown the next page.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The commander was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get to that. Yes, yes. Can we just look, please? What I'm interested in is this -- this information about activities by the 3rd Corps. For example, look at the third paragraph from the top down.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: There's no reference there whatsoever to that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You agree that this is a very small piece of information being submitted to Sarajevo and there is no mention at all of the information that we looked at a while ago; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know where the parties are talking about. Can we be told where to read?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the part that begins with -- that, yes. That is, I think, paragraph number four down under this -- below this title that says "Activities by our Forces."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and then it reads: "In the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, you've seen that, haven't you, the information on the area of responsibility of the 35th Division that you saw earlier on is not included, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes the witness says, "Yes, that's right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say "yes," sir, to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. It's not mentioned there, the information that we looked at a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter says he believes you said "yes." He doesn't -- he didn't hear you say "yes." You can go another two minutes, if you can make use of them. Are you moving to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A different document, Your Honour. The two minutes just won't do, unfortunately. I think it's better to break now, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we stopped for the break when we were dealing with this set of documents. Now I'm going to ask that the witness be shown page 14 of the Bosnian version. Witness, the Prosecutor showed you this document, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is on page 21 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecutor showed you paragraph 3 of this document, Witness, if you'll recall. Can you please look. It's the document talking about the acts by the El Mujahid Detachment. If you can look at it again. Can we look at the English version also. Maybe we can scroll down so we can see the bottom of the page, so Their Honours can follow. Witness, do you agree that here -- can you please look at this excerpt carefully. Can you agree that it says here: "By processing the seized documentation of the 1st Prnjavor Brigade and questioning the prisoners, we learned that the forces have been decimated." In any way, are you able to link these prisoners with the El Mujahid Detachment, based on what is written here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am already going to ask you to remember the date of the document. It's the 2nd of July, and it's in addition to the regular combat report and that it's sent to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the date of the document the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now, at this point of time, be shown page 16 of this document, and page 23 of the English document. The English version is fine. Can we please look at the previous page of the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look to see that this is an act by the General Staff, the Operations, Planning Administration at Kakanj, of the 23rd of July, 1995, and that the document refers to the situation on the front on the 22nd of July, 1995, and do you agree that this act is sent to the president of the Presidency, and it says here to the commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you see that it refers to combat of the 22nd of July, and its characteristics are described here? Now I would like you to look at page 17 of the Bosnian version. That's actually the following page of the Bosnian version and the following page of the English version, too. Can the English version be scrolled down, please, and the Bosnian page is all right. Witness, can you please look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the first sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt my learned colleague. I just want to say for the record this is a series -- or this document or this exhibit appears to constitute -- be constituted out of several documents from the General Staff level. I understand the lines of questioning my learned friend is putting, but I just want to say there are other witnesses from the General Staff Operations and Training Department coming, so maybe these other witnesses would be more suitable witnesses to comment upon these documents, since they're all written on a higher level and are going certainly to another even higher level, the president of the Presidency and so on and so forth. I just wanted to put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just say, this set of documents contains documents that were shown to the witness today, and we are discussing with the witness specifically the information that the witness entered into the document that goes to the General Staff in Kakanj, and I'm asking whether that information that he entered is contained in the documents that are passed on. I'm talking about specific information that is known to the witness, that the witness entered into the document, and I'm just asking the witness whether that piece of information is contained in the information that is passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The problem the Prosecution sees is: How should this witness, who's on the 3rd Corps level, understand what the General Staff officer receiving his document is doing? I think it's more suitable to discuss this line of questioning with a witness who is on that level and who can explain, first of all, to have received the documents from this witness and, secondly, who can then explain in what process he is producing such documents which are sent from the General Staff obviously to a higher level like Presidency and so on. How should this witness, being on the 3rd Corps level, know about the process of what type of information is selected by the General Staff and passed onwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, on your first point, I understood you to say you just wanted to place something on record. You did that. Now you sound like you are objecting. Obviously, if this witness is asked anything he doesn't know, he'll say he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Certainly. I just wanted to put that on the record, that we're not inviting the witness to speculate about what the officers on the General Staff are passing on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When he speculates, stand up and object and say "That's a speculative answer, can the witness answer precisely?" Don't try to prevent him being questioned. If he doesn't know, he'll say he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will do so as advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to say something. I am trying -- I want my learned friends from the Prosecution to understand me. I am trying, with the witnesses, to clarify a situation as much as possible so that I do not have to call witnesses on these circumstances when the time comes for our presentation of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you understood, I'm not asking you about the procedure of forwarding documents. What I'm asking you is about specific information that was in the document that you authored. Does that piece of information appear here? Can you please look at the first sentence under the heading "The Area of Responsibility of the 3rd Corps." The information that you saw earlier referring to the El Mujahedin, does that appear here?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Not dealing with the veracity of this document. The information we sent to the General Staff is not contained in this passage that we're looking at here. The information has to do with the fact that documentation was processed and the captives were questioned. It's obvious that that information is not contained here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now can the witness please look at page 18 of this document. Or rather, Your Honours, perhaps the witness can look at page 19 of the Bosnian version of this set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the page that we are looking at now, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 27 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the Prosecutor showing you this document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First, this is a document of the 23rd of July, 1995. It's an interim operations report. The Trial Chamber noticed something that I also noticed, and I would like you to clarify that here. It is stated here the El Mujahedin detachment, and then it says in this document here Nikolino Brdo where they routed the forces of the Vukovi in fighting conducted on this axis. Chetnik forces from the Vukovi Detachment had losses, 20 Chetniks who remained on our side. Did I read this -- the contents of this document correctly? Please, I don't know -- it seems to me -- I don't know if the translation into English is clear at this point in time, I'm not able to check that, but, please, can you explain, how do you understand "had losses of 20 Chetniks who remained on our side"? Am I right if I understand that dead people remained on our side, the killed bodies of Chetniks, or rather the bodies of killed Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how you understand this document? Look at it again, please.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first thing I wanted to do is when the Prosecutor was putting questions to me about this, I didn't draft this document, but as an officer I can try to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It says that in the course of the day, there were attacks carried out, so from this sentence: "In fighting conducted along this axis, the Chetnik forces of Vukovi had losses, 20 Chetniks who remained on our side," it can be concluded on the basis of that that these 20 Chetniks remained on our side, that we pulled out those dead Chetniks. It says "losses, 20 Chetniks who remained," so now you can ask me if they are alive or dead. But when you say "losses," it would seem to imply that they were killed. This is something that is implied, according to our military logic in reporting. If it says that somebody has losses, immediately the conclusion would be that losses equal death. Had they been captured, then it would have said for sure that such-and-such a number were captured. This is something that would have been emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the only interpretation that can be given to that phrase, when you say "20 Chetniks remained on our side"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "Our side" would imply the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Doesn't it -- couldn't it also mean that 20 standing Chetniks, not dead bodies? They're not saying, "We have 20 bodies," they are saying 20 Chetniks, they remained, "They could have decided to go our way if they wanted to go our way, but of course they would have been shot at if they go our way." What I'm trying to say. Is that the only interpretation that can be given to that phrase? Could it also mean that maybe injured Chetniks, or they may not be injured, they may just be captured, "they are remaining on our side," they are not going away? Dead bodies wouldn't go away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried, as an officer, to explain the terminology that we used in our work. If we would say "losses," then I believe that they were dead. It's possible to speculate as to whether they were that or not. It's something that I cannot know now. But the word "gubitak" would refer to dead Chetniks in our terminology that we used in our reports in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. It's just that the English says "casualties" and casualties could either be dead or injured, couldn't it? Okay. But that's the testimony we're getting. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can correct the translation. This is why I did that, because the English word is not clear. In Bosnian, it is clear, and this is why I actually brought this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Thank you. You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this document, can the witness please look at page 21. We saw this information here that we have just discussed. Now please look at page 21 of the document. Your Honours, in the English it's page 29. Can you please go to the previous page in the Bosnian. Can we zoom in a little bit on this introductory part, if the witness can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see that it's a document of the 24th of July of the Staff of Kakanj, referring to the situation in the field on the 23rd of July, 1995. I'm asking you the same information. It's going out to the president of the Presidency and the army commander. I'm asking you something about a specific information. In this document, can the witness look at the following page, both in the Bosnian and the English versions. Can you please scroll down the English version. Witness, can you please look at the part of the document that talks about the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. This is the fourth or fifth paragraph, where individual corps are referred to.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: As far as that division, there's only one sentence mentioned here, but there's nothing here from the document that we were talking about before. Here it says: "Defence and preparations for further action --"

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the English please move on to the next page. There's the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree, we don't see the same information that was contained in your reports, do we? Fine. Have you answered, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The English, but I haven't seen the Bosnian. I tried to look at the English, but if you could please show the Bosnian too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There's the Bosnian version, the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: There's a single sentence, 37th Division, and then it goes on to explain about the 35th. There's just a single sentence there, it says: "In the area of responsibility of the 35th Division, our forces carried out active defence on the Ozren front." And then preparations for further combat activity, but there's nothing in there, not what we talked about earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. If the witness could please look at page 23 now. 33 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you remember being shown this by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this portion specifically in relation to the El Mujahedin Detachment, the 328th.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Can you now please go to page 26 -- 25, the same document, B/C/S. Just a minute, please. 35 of the English, Your Honours. Your Honours, we have not been able to obtain the entire translation, but we do have the portion that is relevant for our purposes. Witness, can you please look at the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. It's on the next page, the next page of the Bosnian. The next page of the English as well. Again, Witness, please focus on where it says the "3rd Corps." Have a look. You agree that again we don't seem to find the information that we saw in that document a while ago, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No, we don't see that, but we see new information here, the Gornja Blizna area, the reconnaissance and sabotage detachment, the 328th Battalion, a holiday cottage was destroyed where the Chetniks were. It is estimated that between four and five Chetniks were killed. I've actually never seen that information before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. If you can't answer, then what can I be expected to do with it? But I would ask you this: The information that we looked at a while ago, we don't see it here, do we, in this document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right, it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. You agree that the information could have been obtained from a war log or something like that? You don't know. Fine, thanks.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this juncture, Your Honour, can we please have a number for this document, this whole set of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: D446, with all those documents that have been referred to, are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I just make a technical remark, because I saw, while we browsed through the document, that this a compilation -- a set of several documents, and some include documents which have been admitted earlier in the course of the examination-in-chief. So I'm just leaving it here. This -- is it just a technical reason, that this could be dealt with, that we don't admit duplicate translations or documents or split up the documents into numbers 1, 2, 3 or 4. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just add something. It is true, perhaps, one of these documents has been admitted already, but the Defence shall use this document to prove a single fact, a very specific fact by this set of documents provided by the OTP, and then we shall link them up. They go together, some provided by the OTP, some provided by us. It will be very difficult for the Chamber to observe these documents separately, or rather so that we -- or in order for us or the Chamber to look at one exhibit, perhaps the Chamber would have to look at 20 different ones, and that is precisely what I mean. It is in this way that I wish to simplify this to the greatest possible extent. Likewise, Your Honours, you will remember that the OTP introduced large-scale documents, enormous ones, Presidency meetings, in this way, and we, the Defence, raised no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, how big is the document that you wish to admit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forty pages, four or five reports, documents shown by the OTP, and four or five parallel ones, same as we, add to these reports. I even think, Your Honour, it will be much simpler for the Chamber to have it organised in this manner, rather than us tendering them as a series, a sequence of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, the problem we have is that it makes little sense to admit into evidence the same document twice, so our question to you is if you can take away the parts of your document which have already been admitted into evidence and then re-upload the document again so as to have entered into evidence now something only which has not been admitted before. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I'm not sure if I can do it right now, but I could use the next break to do that, and then we can leave this for later, the admission of this document, until the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next break --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. We won't have a chance to do that before tomorrow. Tomorrow, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can do that tomorrow. So what we will do, then, is we admit -- I'm not quite sure which has already been admitted and which has not been admitted here. I seem to think that the document -- the first document of the 19th of July, 1995, has already been admitted, but there may be others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think is the other, but we shall compare, Your Honours. We'll do it all by tomorrow. There's one thing I wish to point out, Your Honours. The OTP also have things organised in this way. I'm just letting my learned friends know, and then I'll be raising the same objections myself. I believe it will be much simpler for the Chamber in the future to follow the facts of the case if this were to be admitted as a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We accept that and hope that you can take away or take out the parts which have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then document 446 is admitted into evidence to the extent that it has not already been admitted, and those portions that have not been admitted yet are to be given one single exhibit number now. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the Defence is ordered to re-upload the documents in such a way that those documents referred to herein which are already exhibits are separated from Exhibit 537. Thank you very much. And a cross-reference is made between the two exhibits. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask you briefly, sir: You mentioned the visit that the commander made to the 3rd Corps. Do you agree that Commander Delic at the time was holding a very high post and that any visit he made, given his position, would have been recorded in the war log or the operations log?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Well, to us General Delic had the same sort of level of prestige as the late President Izetbegovic. Whenever he came, you can easily check this in the operations log and the war log, in the regular reports, but I'm sure this was recorded in the daily reports, that he came to see us, the army commander. He was even in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, any visit he made would have been recorded in the operations log, in the war log, or in the daily report?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, it would have had to be recorded in one of those three documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just ask you briefly about monthly analyses, about some analyses that you testified to, monthly ones. I wish to ask you this: If you look at the initials that a document bears, it's always easy to ascertain who actually wrote the document, whether it was you or another person; would that be right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Monthly analysis is a collective document. If it bears my initials at the end of the document, I mean, I was the one who collected it, who put it together. I would have different departments submitting their contributions to me. My typist would then put this together. I would go through it. When I say "go through it," I mean over the three months of analyses that were shown me. I did those in July, August and September, and I also made daily reports based on whatever developments were taking place. I would make an analysis based on that and then put the whole thing together. Likewise, I would take parts out of it, because these monthly analyses had to be submitted to our subordinate units, and then all of the corps' departments looked at their own sections and contributed. I didn't look at the 35th Division, what they were saying about their logistics, for example, or their intelligence, for that matter. I was an operative officer. I looked at operative matters, and all the other departments did the same thing. They would do their own job, I would do mine. I would put it together. The Department for Planning and Monitoring Combat Operations were away, they were away on the front lines, so I was alone and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please not overlap and please pause between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, Madam Vidovic, the interpreters are complaining. You cut in while the witness was speaking, you overlap, and they don't hear you. They didn't hear the end of the witness's answer, as we can see. He just said: "... So I was alone and ..." and you came in. They didn't -- they missed him. And while I'm speaking, may I just find out from you how much longer you are going to be. I think you've gone far beyond your time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that much, Your Honours, maybe about ten minutes, a total of about ten minutes, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, Your Honours, and the interpreters say that they missed the last bit of your answer, missed it, the transcript. You said I was -- it must have been me who interrupted you by asking another question altogether. You say, "I was alone," and there was something else you wished to add, sir. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: And instead of the Department for Planning and Monitoring Combat Operations, I was the one who produced the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough, thank you. Can the witness now look at PT2361 [Realtime translation read in error "PT2061"].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the document is shown on the monitor, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2361, yes. 2361. It was entered here erroneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before we look at this analysis, I just want to ask you: You worked at the Orahovo IKM in July 1995. I saw that in your statement to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that the IKM Orahovo was formed in order to monitor offensive combat actions according to the plan of operation to unblock Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only reason why it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, this operation to lift the blockade of Sarajevo took place in July of 1995, is that correct, in late July 1991 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No. I think that it began on the 15th of June, the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 15th of June of which year, sir? We have been given two years here, 1995 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, it began on the 15th of June, but it's correct, isn't it, that it continued throughout July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It's like this: We formed the forward command post in the village of Orahovo in order to lift the blockade of Sarajevo in the beginning of June. On the 1st or the 2nd of June, we were already up there. Ten to 15 days before the start of the operation, the IKM was formed and we were staying up there. I was up there until about the 10th, 12th or the 15th of July, 1995. We're now talking about 1995. And after that, I asked to be relieved to go back because I had had enough, I was tired. I wanted to be replaced by my officer Safet Sivro, which is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the gist of my question was not about where you were, but the actual operation itself continued throughout July 1995; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The operation started in -- on the 15th of June, 1995, and it went on, and the IKM was there also until the end of July. The IKM was closed down only in early August.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you very much. Can the witness now look at page 2 of this analysis for July 1995. Can you please look. Can we also see the English version, please. Can you look at the part of the section for planning and tracking of combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says in this part here that has to do with the planning section that the focus of the work of the planning section in the month of July was to monitor offensive combat actions according to the plan of Operation T, and it says "the Sarajevo theatre"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the 3rd Corps, according to this document, seems not to have prepared or planned combat actions in July concerning the Vozuca-Ozren section?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Not the Command of the Corps, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, this would be something that would be referred to in a document of this nature?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Corps and the bulk of the Command was actually at Orahovo, and it was monitoring the Sarajevo operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point I would like the witness again to look at Exhibit 494. While we're waiting for the document, and we have it here on the screen:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that the Prosecutor showed you this document earlier today? It has to do with the execution of combat actions according to the order of the Army General Staff. Do you remember that you testified about this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be -- and before it's actually put away, Witness, please:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that the order is mentioned here? You actually told us. You testified about the order of the 3rd Corps. You recollect that in relation to this order?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document be put away. And before this hearing today, the Prosecutor presented to us the order. It's very brief. We didn't have time to translate it at all, but we copied the order, and we have distributed the Bosnian version. We have given it to the interpreters. I would like -- oh, actually, we didn't even manage to do that, Your Honours. Perhaps the document can be placed on the ELMO. I'm going to ask the witness slowly to read the document. It's a short document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can maybe just assist, because I managed to get an urgent translation, which is unofficial. It says "Draft Translation." It was done -- the document came in this morning. It has no ERN number yet to it, but it's the best, I think, CLSS translator who's working with the OTP has produced it. It's still a draft, but it's better than nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that if it is a short document, maybe the interpreters can interpret it for us. We don't need that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we are going to submit a translation later. I would be grateful to the Prosecution if they would give me that translation. What I would like to ask you is to just scroll down the document so that the witness can see whose document it is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see -- are you able to read this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you slowly read, slowly, so that the interpreters and the transcript can keep up.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: "Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Command of the 3rd Corps. Strictly confidential number 02/3-2," should be "2", and that's the Operations Centre number, "-501. Zenica, the 17th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be scrolled down so that the witness can continue.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Heading: "Execution of Active Combat Actions. Order sent --" should I continue to read the order?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: "The situation around Zepa is quite favourable in the military sense. However, certain circumstances, strong Chetniks forces, action by Chetnik Air Force, the sense of being closed in, the duration of carrying out combat actions and similar, are having an effect on the morale of the combat personnel who have a sense of being abandoned. For the purpose of assistance and easing the situation around the front -- on the front around Zepa and pursuant to order of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 1/825-1306, dated the 17th of July, 1995, and the order of the 3rd Corps Command, strictly confidential number 02/3-2-500, dated the 17th of July, 1995, I hereby order: "1. Immediately undertake active combat on the entire front in your zones on selected axes and facilities. 2. The commanders of divisions and brigades are personally responsible to me for the implementation of these assignments. 3. The report pursuant to this order should be delivered to me by 1800 hours of the 18th of July, 1995, with activities described in detail." Initials "NP/0N" for the commander, Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic, sent to the 35th and the 37th Division, the 319th Liberation Brigade, 303rd Vitez Brigade, and the 330th Light Brigade, and for the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. This "NP," these are your initials?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And is this the document you told us that you drafted in relation to the General Staff order? You testified about that earlier today?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I probably wrote it on the basis of the order, because I mentioned the order 1306 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do mention it.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Then that would be it. There is also another order from the Corps Command of the day before dated the 16th. So on the basis of those two orders, we issued this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now in connection with this, do you agree that it states here that these subordinate units should select the axes and facilities that they would act on?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: The sense of the first paragraph is to immediately undertake active combat in their zones on selected axes and facilities. That would indicate that they already should have known where they were supposed to go. The word "isabrani," [phoen] "selected," indicates that this was in the past, that it had already been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you worked on these types of documents. Do you recall that the action -- July action in --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not Sarajevo. I am talking about the July action in the Ozren-Vozuca front. Do you recall if the corps ever issued an order specifically for that front or whether that was done at the level of the division, if you're able to help us?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Please believe me, I don't know. We were all engaged on Sarajevo. As far as I know, in Sarajevo we were not thinking of making orders for Vozuca, not for Vozuca, but for other areas or for areas of responsibility of other units. I would probably know and remember if we were drafting orders at the IKM, because that's when the complete Corps Command was there at that time, except for 10 or 15 officers who stayed behind in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you very much. We clarified that sufficiently. I'm just going to put one more question to you. And before that, Your Honours, please, if this document can be given an exhibit number, and we are going to do our best to furnish you with a translation and to submit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. And in the meantime, Madam Vidovic, you have now used 19 of your 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It should be "39," Madam Registrar. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that I will need just one more minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you were shown a document, the document E535, which mentioned the briefing, if you recall, of the assistant commanders from the 11th of September until the 18th of September, 1995, and it had to do with Perici. Do you recall that document so I don't have to show it to you? It spoke about those 100 Chetniks that were encircled, and I just want to ask you one question about that. Please, did you ever, after that, receive any kind of information that would indicate that any of those people were captured?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: No. I would probably have remembered that. It's quite a significant matter, and I would have remembered it. I remember many things from the time of the war, but this is something that I really do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Given the advanced stage of time, and the Judges want to ask questions as well, I have just one or two clarifying questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were you, in the Operations Centre, ever involved in planning of combat operations or was this another unit's domain?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Specifically, orders were drafted by the Department for Planning and Monitoring Combat Operations. My own desk officer, Captain Mirsad Caluk, was involved in the work of that section. He was the graphic designer. He would produce documents for them, a draftsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Mirsad Caluk would then know how the planning would take place and how approvals about combat operations of subordinate units were given in the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: I'm not certain that he would, specifically what you're asking me about. I'm not certain he could answer your question. He was just a draftsman. He drew whatever he was told to draw, "Draw this, draw that." He had no influence over who was giving specific orders to units. He just drew for them, and that was the involvement of my own department, the Operations Centre, in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the involvement of your department was that for the planning process, maps were drawn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but in order to plan for the establishment of forward command posts, we, as a sector, as a department, would always get involved, which means both me and my two desk officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have just looked at the last exhibit, which was in B/C/S lying next to you here. I want to show you Exhibit 443. You see it's a document from the 18th of July, and it's sent to the Command of the 3rd Corps. Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the numbers here in the first line, they refer to this General Staff order 825-1306. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And they also refer to the order, if you could confirm this, which you just read out. It's 501. That's the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: That's the order you have just seen; yeah?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain, what is the 35th Division doing here in relation to your order which you drafted and which you have seen a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: First of all, during the proofing I explained to you that this was an error. It says: "Pursuant to an order of the General Staff, the army," and then the number of the General Staff, so whoever did this in the 35th Division just copied this from my order. He said, "All right, I invoke this and that order," and then he invokes it. I can't say illiterate, but certainly not very accurate. He simply didn't have the order in his hands. I've already explained that, didn't I, the reporting on what they will do. Our orders, as far as I can remember, were for combat operations to start being launched as soon as possible along such axes as had been selected and in their own areas, and then they are reporting, based on the previous order, what they are doing. It's their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that they're responding to your order?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN PESTO
utterances.text: Yes. It says in the header.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. Judge. Thank you very much. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, sir. We just take this opportunity to say thank you to you for taking the time off to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. May you have a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope that my evidence will contribute to establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it brings us to virtually the end of the day. There's no point calling a new witness. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, same court. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of October, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
